subject: Angina
object: a feeling of pain or tightness, usually in the chest.
source_quote: Angina is a feeling of pain or tightness, usually in your chest.

subject: The main symptom of angina
object: sudden pain in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arms.
source_quote: The main symptom of angina is sudden pain in your chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arms.

subject: Angina pain
object: like tightness, squeezing, pressure or a dull ache, and may make the person feel sick, breathless, dizzy or sweaty.
source_quote: Symptoms of angina The pain may: feel like tightness, squeezing or pressure, or like a dull ache make you feel sick, breathless, dizzy or sweaty

subject: Angina episodes
object: exercise, stress, emotion or cold temperatures, although sometimes there is no obvious trigger.
source_quote: Symptoms of angina They are often brought on by exercise, stress, emotion or cold temperatures – although sometimes there's no obvious trigger.

subject: Angina attacks
object: less than 10 minutes and should stop after a few minutes of rest or taking angina medicine.
source_quote: Angina attacks usually last less than 10 minutes and should stop after resting for a few minutes or taking your angina medicine.

subject: People already diagnosed with angina who develop chest pain
object: stop and rest, use the prescribed medicine, usually glyceryl trinitrate, and take a second dose after 5 minutes if the first does not help; if symptoms persist 5 minutes after the second dose, call 999 for an ambulance.
source_quote: If you've been diagnosed with angina and get chest pain, follow the instructions you've been given for treating your angina: Stop what you're doing and rest. Use any medicine you've been prescribed – this is usually glyceryl trinitrate (GTN). Take another dose after 5 minutes if the first dose does not help. If you still have symptoms 5 minutes after taking the 2nd dose, call 999 for an ambulance.

subject: The NHS angina emergency advice
object: diagnosed angina with chest pain not stopping after a few minutes of rest or angina medicine; sudden persistent chest pain or discomfort like squeezing, pressure, burning or indigestion; pain spreading to either arm, neck, jaw, shoulder, stomach or back; or chest pain with sweating, sickness, lightheadedness or breathlessness; this could be a heart attack needing immediate hospital treatment, so do not drive yourself to A&E and the 999 call-handler will advise what to do.
source_quote: Angina Immediate action required: Call 999 now if: you've been diagnosed with angina and have chest pain that does not stop after resting for a few minutes or after taking your angina medicine you get sudden pain or discomfort in your chest that does not go away – the pain can feel like squeezing or pressure inside your chest, burning or indigestion you get pain that spreads to your left or right arm, or your neck, jaw, shoulder, stomach or back you have chest pain and you feel sweaty, sick, light-headed or short of breath You could be having a heart attack. Call 999 straight away as you need immediate treatment in hospital. Do not drive yourself to A&E. The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

subject: People with chest pain or other angina symptoms that come and go, or diagnosed angina that is worse, more frequent, longer-lasting or occurs at rest,
object: by calling 111 or using 111 online.
source_quote: Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if: you have chest pain or other symptoms of angina that come and go you've been diagnosed with angina and it feels worse than before, is happening more often, lasts longer or happens when you're resting You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

subject: If a GP thinks someone may have angina,
object: to a heart specialist, a cardiologist.
source_quote: If a GP thinks you may have angina, you'll be referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist).

subject: Tests for angina
object: blood tests, an ECG to check cardiac electrical activity, measurement of blood oxygen and scans such as an angiogram, MRI or CT.
source_quote: Angina What happens at your GP appointment You may have tests including: blood tests an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the electrical activity of your heart checking the level of oxygen in your blood scans, such as an angiogram, MRI scan or CT scan

subject: Angina
object: the heart does not receive enough blood, usually because coronary heart disease narrows or blocks its supplying vessels with fatty deposits, but it can also be caused by heart vessels tightening inappropriately, causing vasospastic or microvascular angina.
source_quote: Angina happens when the heart does not get enough blood. This is usually due to coronary heart disease, where the blood vessels supplying blood to the heart become narrowed or blocked by fatty deposits. But it can also be caused by the blood vessels in your heart tightening when they should not (vasospastic angina or microvascular angina).

subject: Angina
object: men aged 45 or over, women aged 55 or over, smokers, people drinking more than 14 alcohol units weekly, people with obesity or overweight, high blood pressure or high cholesterol, previous heart problems such as heart attack or arrhythmia, close relatives with heart problems, or another condition such as diabetes, arthritis or kidney disease.
source_quote: You're more likely to get angina if you: are a man aged 45 or over, or a woman aged 55 or over smoke drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week are living with obesity or overweight have high blood pressure or high cholesterol have had heart problems before, like a heart attack or heart rhythm problem (arrhythmia) have close relatives who have heart problems have another condition, such as diabetes, arthritis or kidney disease

subject: People with angina
object: treat an attack with glyceryl trinitrate, reduce the chance of an attack with medicines such as beta blockers, or reduce stroke or heart-attack risk with medicines such as low-dose aspirin or statins.
source_quote: If you have angina, you may be given medicine to: treat an angina attack if you have one (glyceryl trinitrate) lower your chances of having an angina attack, such as beta blockers reduce your risk of having a stroke or heart attack, such as low-dose aspirin or statins

subject: People with angina
object: surgery to increase blood flow to the heart, using coronary angioplasty or a coronary artery bypass.
source_quote: Treatment for angina Sometimes you may be recommended to have surgery to increase the blood flow to your heart (coronary angioplasty or a coronary artery bypass).

subject: Angina
object: heart attack or stroke, making treatment and healthy lifestyle changes important to reduce that risk.
source_quote: Having angina means you're at higher risk of having a heart attack or stroke. It's important to treat it and make healthy lifestyle changes to reduce this risk.

subject: With treatment, angina symptoms
object: over time and may eventually stop.
source_quote: How angina affects your life With treatment, the symptoms should improve over time and may eventually stop.

subject: If angina symptoms are well controlled, angina
object: a major impact on life, and most activities, including exercise and sex, can usually continue.
source_quote: If your symptoms are well controlled, angina will not usually have a big impact on your life. You'll usually be able to continue with most things, including exercise and sex.

subject: Around half of people with angina undergoing elective coronary angiography
relation: have no obstructive epicardial coronary disease;
object: this large heterogeneous chronic coronary syndrome includes distinct vasomotor disorders, with microvascular and/or vasospastic angina the two most common underlying coronary functional disorders in the INOCA population.
source: Article: Ford TJ, Berry C. Angina: contemporary diagnosis and management. Heart 2020
source_quote: Around half of all patients with angina undergoing elective coronary angiography have no obstructive epicardial CAD. This large, heterogeneous chronic coronary syndrome is comprised of distinct vasomotor disorders including microvascular angina (MVA) and/or vasospastic angina (VSA)—the two most common underlying disorders of coronary vascular function in the INOCA population.

subject: Angina
object: a relative deficiency of myocardial oxygen supply, meaning ischaemia, and typically follows activity or physiological stress.
source: Article: Ford TJ, Berry C. Angina: contemporary diagnosis and management. Heart 2020
source_quote: Typically, angina involves a relative deficiency of myocardial oxygen supply (ie, ischaemia) and typically occurs after activity or physiological stress (box 1).

subject: Coronary vasospastic angina
object: transient, reversible coronary vasoconstriction that leads to myocardial ischaemia.
source: Article: Rehan R, Weaver J, Yong A. Coronary Vasospastic Angina: A Review of the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management. Life 2022
source_quote: Coronary vasospastic angina (VSA) is characterised by transient and reversible vasoconstriction of the coronary vasculature leading to myocardial ischemia.

subject: Vasospastic angina
object: with or without atherosclerosis, affecting epicardial coronary arteries or the microvasculature.
source: Article: Rehan R, Weaver J, Yong A. Coronary Vasospastic Angina: A Review of the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management. Life 2022
source_quote: VSA is a heterogeneous phenomenon that can occur in patients with or without atherosclerosis and affects the epicardial coronary arteries or microvasculature.

subject: Vasospastic angina
object: impaired coronary vasomotion (physiological rhythmic contractions) in one or more coronary arteries, with vascular smooth-muscle-cell dysfunction coupled with a predominance of vasoconstrictive metabolites playing an additional role; a localised vasomotion abnormality may cause focal (segmental) spasm in a coronary artery, while a more diffuse abnormality may cause multivessel spasm.
source: Article: Rehan R, Weaver J, Yong A. Coronary Vasospastic Angina: A Review of the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management. Life 2022
source_quote: The pathophysiology of VSA is characterised by an impairment of vasomotion (physiological rhythmical contractions) in one or more coronary arteries . In addition, vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) dysfunction, coupled with a predominance of vasoconstrictive metabolites, plays an adjunctive role . A localised vasomotion abnormality may produce focal (segmental) spasm in a coronary artery, while a more diffuse abnormality may result in multivessel spasm .

subject: The variable clinical spectrum of vasospastic angina
object: transient, non-exertional, nitrate-responsive angina tending to occur at night or early in the morning.
source: Article: Rehan R, Weaver J, Yong A. Coronary Vasospastic Angina: A Review of the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management. Life 2022
source_quote: The clinical spectrum of VSA is variable but essentially includes a transient, non-exertional, nitrate-responsive angina that tends to occur at night or in the early morning.

subject: The natural history of vasospastic angina
relation: remains a topic of discussion, and
object: absence of anginal symptoms may not always indicate a benign prognosis because many such patients have silent myocardial ischaemia; these patients can have prolonged bouts of vasospasm, leading to atherosclerosis progression, thrombus formation and ultimately myocardial infarction.
source: Article: Rehan R, Weaver J, Yong A. Coronary Vasospastic Angina: A Review of the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management. Life 2022
source_quote: Interestingly, the natural history of VSA remains a topic of discussion. Given the presence of silent myocardial ischemia in many such patients, a lack of anginal symptoms may not always indicate a benign prognosis. Furthermore, such patients can suffer prolonged bouts of vasospasm, leading to the progression of atherosclerosis, thrombus formation, and eventually myocardial infarction .
